passage:
Dear Gopika,
Remember I told you I'd give the statistics course one star on the feedback form? I nearly did. The last three weeks were awful: the professor rushed through regression, cancelled two classes, and the final assignment was confusing. So I sat down, still angry, and started typing "worst course ever."
Then I opened my notebook from the start of the term. In July he explained probability with cricket scores, and for the first time in my life maths made sense. In August he stayed back every Friday for doubts. My notes from those weeks are full of stars and "finally!!"
It was a good course with a bad ending. I'd almost rated only the ending.
I gave it four stars, with a comment about the last month.
Harsha

qa.q: How many classes did the professor cancel in the last three weeks?
qa.a: He cancelled two classes.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when starting to type "worst course ever"?
qa.a: Harsha felt angry and frustrated, with the last three bad weeks filling the whole memory of the course.

qa.q: What helped Harsha rate the course fairly, and why?
qa.a: Opening the notebook from the start of term, which brought back the good months so the rating reflected the whole course, not just the end.

qa.q: How might the professor see a one-star rating if Harsha had sent it?
qa.a: The professor might feel it was unfair, since the early months had clearly helped Harsha understand maths.

grounding: A student's letter shows nearly rating a course only by its last weeks, until old notes bring back the good months.

passage: Manjula, I have to confess something about the peer evaluations. So, I'm Kishore, and we had to rate our project teammates out of ten. I gave the quiet guy, Ravi, a four. I was so sure. In the last two weeks he missed a meeting and sent his section late. That's all I could think about. Then last night I scrolled back through our group chat, all the way to January. Ravi built the whole survey. He fixed my code in February at midnight. He found the dataset we used. For three months he was the best on the team. Two bad weeks, and I'd forgotten all of it. I've asked the professor if I can change my rating. Honestly, I was rating the last fortnight, not the person.

qa.q: What score did Kishore first give Ravi?
qa.a: A four.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when first rating Ravi?
qa.a: Kishore felt sure and annoyed, because the missed meeting and late section in the last two weeks were all that came to mind.

qa.q: What did Kishore do to correct the rating, and why was it fairer?
qa.a: Kishore scrolled back through the group chat to January and asked to change the score, judging all three months instead of the last two weeks.

qa.q: How might Ravi feel if he saw the first rating?
qa.a: Ravi would probably feel hurt and misjudged, after building the survey and fixing code at midnight.

grounding: A student admits rating a teammate by the last two weeks, forgetting months of strong work, then asking to change the score.

passage:
Week 12, Monday. The hostel committee asked Arnab to rate the mess contractor for the year. Last week the dal had been watery twice and there was a hair in the rice. "Two out of ten," Arnab said to Neelam, the mess secretary. "They're terrible."
Week 12, Wednesday. Neelam brought him the complaint register for the whole year. In the first nine months: three complaints. The food had been hot, on time, and there had been special meals on festival days. The bad run had started only after the head cook left three weeks ago.
Week 13, Monday. Arnab rewrote his rating: "Seven out of ten for the year. Last month poor, since the head cook left. Please fix." Neelam smiled. "That's the first review I can actually use."

qa.q: How many complaints were in the register for the first nine months?
qa.a: Three complaints.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he said "Two out of ten"?
qa.a: He felt irritated and disgusted, with last week's watery dal and the hair in the rice filling his whole view of the year.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that helped Arnab rate fairly?
qa.a: She brought the complaint register for the whole year, showing the bad run only started when the head cook left.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Arnab's rewritten rating?
qa.a: Neelam sees it as useful, because it rates the whole year and points to the real recent problem.

grounding: Shows a student rating a mess contractor by the last few weeks, until a year-long record changes his score.

passage: At the women's dairy cooperative in Anand district, Aditi had been the young manager for a year. Review time came in March, and her first thought about Sarita, the collection supervisor, was the mess in February: two days of spoiled milk when a chiller broke. That was all she could remember. But Aditi had a habit. Every month she wrote a few lines in a green register about each supervisor. She sat under the neem tree and read Sarita's page. April: trained six new collectors. June: stayed till midnight during the monsoon flooding. September: found the fault in the testing machine. December: collection up by a tenth. February: chiller problem, not her fault, but slow to report it. Aditi wrote the review: "An excellent year. One lesson: report equipment faults at once." Sarita read it twice and smiled.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt reading the review?

grounding: Shows a fair manager using monthly notes so a performance review reflects the whole year, not just the most recent problem.

passage: In the Madrid office, performance reviews were due on Friday. Ines, a new team manager, sat down to write Layla's. Her mind went straight to November: Layla had missed a deadline, and a client had complained. It felt like the whole story. But in January Ines had started a small habit: a note on her phone after each week, a line per person. She opened it. February: Layla stayed late to finish the pitch. April: suggested the new filing system everyone now uses. July: covered for two colleagues on leave. September: best client feedback in the team. November: missed deadline; she had been sick that week, Ines now remembered. Ines deleted her first draft. The new one began: "A strong year with one difficult month." qa.q: What was Ines feeling when she first thought of Layla's review?

qa.a: A weekly note on her phone for each person, which gives a record of the whole year so recent events don't dominate.

grounding: Shows a fair manager using weekly notes so a performance review reflects the whole year, not just the latest memory.

passage: On the first day of Class 5, a new boy called Hemant came in late, dropped his bag loudly and laughed when the teacher said his name wrong. Class 4 observation note, 25 July.
Harish joined us three weeks ago. On his first day he cried at lunch, and some children, Chinmay among them, called him "a baby."
Since then he has settled well. He scored highest in the maths quiz, he organised a game of kho-kho at break, and he stood up for a younger child in the corridor. Yet today, when I asked Chinmay to pair with Harish for the science project, he said, "Not with the baby." When I asked why, he said, "He cries." I asked when. "On the first day." Nothing since.

qa.a: Harish might feel hurt and stuck, since he has done so much since then and is still judged by one hard day.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child still judging a new classmate by his first-day tears, though later behaviour is very different.

passage: The power had gone out at nine, and Kishore's history exam was at eight the next morning. passage: In the Mumbai flat, Vikas was revising the twelve steps of the nitrogen cycle for his biology test. He read the list from the top every time. Dear Shalini,
Something interesting happened at my cousin's matchmaking meeting on Sunday. I went along for moral support.
The young man arrived twenty minutes late because of a bus breakdown and walked in flustered, apologising, sweat on his collar. I could see my aunt's face close. After that, everything he said sounded wrong to her. He was actually warm and funny, asked good questions, and spoke kindly about his mother. But on the drive home, my aunt only talked about the lateness and the sweat.
My cousin, though, said, "I liked him once he calmed down." She's asked for a second meeting, at a café near his office, so he won't have to rush.
It made me think about first minutes. They're so heavy, and so unfair.
Nikita

passage: Sarika, you won't believe what I watched yesterday. I'm Jatin, right, and my flatmate had his big online interview. I was in the room, quiet, doing my own work. passage: When Omkar joined our design team last year, I disliked him within a day. I'm Minakshi, and I'm not proud of it. Our new trainee, Trisha, started on Monday. My honest first impression: disinterested. She yawned in the induction and barely asked questions.

Vaibhav's eighth birthday party was yesterday. Most of the afternoon was lovely: treasure hunt, drawing, a magic trick by his uncle, lemonade on the terrace. passage: My son Akash visits me every Sunday, and I learned something from my own mother about how to end those visits. I'm Rukmini, and for years I let our Sundays end in a rush: dishes in the sink, me reminding him about his taxes, him checking the time. He'd leave looking tired. One day I realised he probably remembered those last ten minutes more than the lovely lunch. So I changed the ending. Now, before he leaves, we sit on the balcony with tea for five minutes. I tell him one thing I loved about the day. I pack him leftovers with a small note. No reminders, no lists. I say the hard things earlier, over lunch. Last week he said, "Amma, I look forward to Sundays more now." I think it's the ending.

qa.q: What does Rukmini pack for Akash when he leaves?
qa.a: Leftovers with a small note.

qa.a: She felt sorry and concerned, realising he probably remembered the rushed last minutes more than the lovely lunch.

qa.a: She ends with tea, one thing she loved about the day and a note, moving hard topics earlier, so the visit finishes warmly.

qa.a: Akash seems happier, saying he looks forward to Sundays more.
